claims.text: The high-temperature structural and chemical stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by configurational-entropy stabilization.
Configurational-entropy stabilization promotes chemical and structural homogeneity in a solid solution.
Systematically changing the number and composition of constituent elements while retaining near-equiatomic ratios changes the nanoparticles' configurational entropy.
Catalytic service temperatures of interest are 773–1173 K.
Thermoelectric service temperatures of interest are 473–1923 K.
Higher configurational entropy reduces the thermodynamic driving force for phase segregation.
Higher configurational entropy thermodynamically stabilizes a single-phase solid-solution structure at elevated temperature.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing more elements will resist phase segregation better than lower-configurational-entropy nanoparticles.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing more elements will retain greater structural stability at elevated temperatures.
Near-equiatomic nanoparticles containing more elements will retain greater chemical stability at elevated temperatures.
Nanoparticles with fewer elements or non-equiatomic compositions have lower configurational entropy than the proposed higher-element, near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
Lower-configurational-entropy nanoparticles are more susceptible to phase segregation under otherwise identical conditions.
The proposed entropy-stabilization relationship applies only when atomic-size mismatch and electronegativity differences permit formation of a single-phase solid solution.
Diffusion rates and other kinetic factors can affect high-temperature phase stability and introduce variability.
